subject: Business Models
title: Skype's Freemium Breakthrough
description: A micro-lesson that makes Skype's Freemium Breakthrough usable.

hook.text: Skype gave away free internet calls. Within 2 years, 100 million people used it. Very few paid.

buildup.text: Free Skype-to-Skype calls attracted users. SkypeOut charged for calls to real phone numbers.

discovery.text: Even with less than 10% conversion, Skype hit $860 million in revenue. Scale compensates for low conversion.

twist.text: Microsoft bought Skype for $8.5 billion, then watched Zoom eat its market with a better freemium model.

climax.text: Skype proved freemium works at scale but also showed that free users move to whoever offers better free.

punchline.text: $8.5 billion purchase, lost to Zoom. Free users have zero loyalty.

quiz.question: Why did Skype lose to Zoom despite having 100M+ users?
options: Zoom offered a better freemium experience

details.summary: Skype's 2003 launch offered free voice and video calls over the internet, attracting hundreds of millions of users while monetizing through paid features like calling landlines and premium business accounts. It demonstrated how freemium could disrupt a trillion-dollar telecommunications industry.
details.whyItMatters: Skype proved that freemium could work at massive scale in a market dominated by incumbents charging per minute. By making the core product free, Skype attracted 660 million users in under a decade.
takeaways: Free internet calls attracted hundreds of millions of users globally
Paid calls to landlines and phones monetized a fraction of the user base
Microsoft acquired Skype for 8.5 billion dollars in 2011

faq.question: How did Skype's freemium model disrupt telecommunications?
faq.answer: By making internet-to-internet calls free, Skype eliminated the per-minute revenue model that telecom companies depended on. Users switched long-distance and international calls to Skype, destroying telecom pricing power. Carriers were forced to offer unlimited calling plans in response.

faq.question: What happened to Skype after its freemium success?
faq.answer: eBay acquired Skype for 2.6 billion dollars in 2005, then sold it to investors before Microsoft bought it for 8.5 billion in 2011. Microsoft integrated Skype into its enterprise offerings, but Zoom eventually outcompeted it by offering a better freemium video experience.
